column4: Pharaoh's household picks up the exposed infant, so the source dictionary's آل as a returning household meets the found child's entry into the very house that threatens his people.
This ayah identifies those welcomed in 59:9 as poor emigrants expelled from their homes and property, supplying the homelessness and need to which the host household responds.
When parents reach old age in one's care, the grown child must neither rebuke nor repel them but speak nobly; this is the section's reversal from being raised to sheltering one's former carers.
Noah is told to carry his family into the ark except those already excluded, making the vessel a household refuge while marking that refuge's divinely set boundary.
A father entrusting another son says that God is the best guardian and most merciful, closely matching the section's claim that the vulnerable child ultimately has a Lord beyond human carers.
Joseph commands his brothers to bring their whole family to him, initiating the household reunion completed when he shelters his parents in 12:99.
After recalling his flight in fear, Moses says his Lord gave him judgment and made him a messenger; divine formation answers Pharaoh's claim in 26:18 that Pharaoh's house made him.
As a displaced fugitive heading toward Midian, Moses asks his Lord to guide him on the right way; that guidance leads into the receiving household of 28:23-27.
The ayah states that God is the one who enriches and grants sufficiency, a repeated direct formulation of the Lord's act in finding the poor person and enriching him.
Human beings are created in their mothers' wombs “creation after creation,” a particularly close Quranic formulation of the source dictionary's stage-by-stage nurture toward completion.
Mary's mother entrusts the child still in her womb wholly to her Lord, beginning the passage in which a child is received, raised, and assigned a guardian.
At Mary's birth her mother names her and commends her and her descendants to God's protection, supplying the parental act of entrustment that precedes the foster care of 3:37.

Immediately after witnessing provision in his foster child's chamber, Zechariah asks his Lord for good offspring, making care of another's child and hope for one's own meet in a single household passage.
The angels answer Zechariah with news of John while he stands praying, showing the guardian's own household enlarged by a divinely granted child.
God makes the House a place to which people return and a place of security, a public sacred counterpart to the section's home defined by mutual return and refuge.
Moses' mother's heart becomes empty after separation and nearly reveals him until God steadies her, exposing the wound that the return in 28:13 heals.
The mother sends Moses' sister to trace him from a distance, and the child's family quietly maintains connection before the foster-household offer in 28:12.
Moses accepts the marriage-and-service arrangement without injustice between the two terms and makes God witness, completing the fair household compact begun in 28:27.
The father seeks a solemn pledge that his son will be brought back unless the brothers are overpowered, showing a human guardian trying to secure the child's return while admitting his limits.
Joseph answers the brothers who expelled him with no reproach and a prayer for mercy, supplying the softened heart that permits the family's later return into his care.
After the bonds created by migration, shelter, and aid, blood relatives are declared closer to one another in the legal order, marking a boundary between received communal kinship and lineage.
The Prophet's wives receive the relational title of believers' mothers while blood relatives retain priority in law, another precise boundary around nonbiological household belonging.
One soul, its mate, and the many men and women spread from the pair give a Quranic account of the household expanding through marriage and kinship.
The marriage ruling repeatedly uses the language of chastity and being guarded, giving lexical substance to the source dictionary's statement that marriage is a fortress for the unmarried.
From created humanity God establishes both blood lineage and marriage ties, distinguishing the two relations through which the section's house grows.
God makes human houses places of rest, stating directly the sheltering function that the section's received child discovers in a home.
One created state is transformed into another through embryo, bones, flesh, and a new creation, an extended concrete parallel to raising something state by state.
People are invited to spend yet some withhold, while God is rich and they are poor; the poor householder's dependence therefore does not cancel the call to give.
Vessels and cups are circulated among the blessed; read with the youths identified in 76:19, this supplies the objects handed in the section's secondary child-service scene.
The silver-crystal vessels are measured exactly, adding the prepared household service whose attendants appear in 76:19.
In the spending passage, Satan threatens poverty while God promises forgiveness and bounty; fear of becoming poor is exposed as a force that can close the providing hand.
After 31:14 recalls parental nurture, this ayah refuses obedience when parents demand idolatry yet still commands kind worldly companionship, setting a boundary without dissolving care.
The correction asks whether the blind visitor might purify himself, identifying moral possibility in the vulnerable person whom 80:1-2 slighted.
The blind visitor may receive a reminder that benefits him, completing why turning away from him mistakes his worth.
A caravan finds a hidden boy and greets him as merchandise rather than making him family, a dark counter-scene to finding the vulnerable child and sheltering him.
Joseph is sold for a paltry price after being found, showing the child commodified before the receiving household of 12:21 gives him an honored lodging.
Immediately after failing to honor the orphan and feed the poor, people consume inheritance greedily; the ayah shows how the closed household can turn a vulnerable person's estate into prey.
God alone is ٱلْقَاهِرُ over His servants; this different Quranic use of the source's qahr root marks the boundary between divine sovereignty and the human domination forbidden toward an orphan.
The repeated statement that God is the Subduer over His servants reinforces that ultimate qahr belongs to God, while the receiving house is commanded to renounce humiliating power over the child.
Some spouses and children can become enemies, yet believers are told to pardon and forgive; the ayah both limits idealized household safety and preserves the softened response.
Wealth and children are a trial rather than possessions that guarantee honor, placing a boundary around the expanding, provisioned household of the section.
The act of frowning and turning away is a close behavioral reverse of receiving a vulnerable person with the softened heart developed in the section.
This ayah identifies the person slighted in 80:1 as blind, making the reversal concern an actual dependent seeker rather than discourtesy in the abstract.
On that day a person flees from his brother, reversing the household whose members ordinarily return to and support one another.
Flight extends to mother and father, setting an eschatological limit on the parent-child care that the section traces across generations.
Spouse and children complete the household from which each person flees, the full reverse of marriage enlarging a sheltering home.
The comparison to hidden pearls may echo the source dictionary's explicit “unique pearl” valuation, though this ayah applies the pearl image to heavenly companions rather than to a solitary child.
